pos: n. pl. (the golden trays that received the burnt wick-ends trimmed from the candlestick; Hebrew machtah)
etymology: English snuff, the charred end of a wick, + dish. The snuffers cut the spent wick; the snuffdish caught it. Both were of pure gold.
biblical_def: Of the candlestick the LORD said, “And the tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, shall be of pure gold” (Exo 25:38). Bezaleel obeyed: “And he made his seven lamps, and his snuffers, and his snuffdishes, of pure gold” (Exo 37:23). When the camp moved, the Kohathites covered the lamp and “his tongs, and his snuffdishes, and all the oil vessels thereof, wherewith they minister unto it” (Num 4:9). The dish that held the burnt refuse of the sanctuary light was gold because it belonged to the pattern, and the pattern was not Moses' to improve: “And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount” (Exo 25:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a snuff as the burning or burnt part of a candle-wick, and a snuffdish as the vessel appointed to receive what the snuffers take away.
webster_full: SNUFF, n. The burning part of a candle or lamp wick, or the part which has been burnt.
SNUFFERS, n. plu. An instrument for cropping the snuff of a candle.
DISH, n. A broad open vessel, made of various materials, used for serving up meat and various kinds of food at the table.
scriptures: And the tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, shall be of pure gold.
And he made his seven lamps, and his snuffers, and his snuffdishes, of pure gold.
Num 4:9
And they shall take a cloth of blue, and cover the candlestick of the light, and his lamps, and his tongs, and his snuffdishes, and all the oil vessels thereof, wherewith they minister unto it:
And look that thou make them after their pattern, which was shewed thee in the mount.
corruption_summary: The golden snuffdish is the standing rebuke to the notion that the small and unseen parts of worship are ours to arrange as we please.
corruption_paragraphs: Nothing in the tabernacle was too small to be commanded. The tray that caught a burnt wick-end was specified by God and made of pure gold, and it travelled wrapped in blue cloth on the shoulders of Kohath. This is the regulative principle in miniature. God did not give Moses a purpose and leave him the means; He gave the pattern down to the snuffdish, and Hebrews 8:5 says the reason — the whole was “the example and shadow of heavenly things.” A worship whose visible parts are commanded and whose small parts are invented is not the worship of Exodus 25.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Exodus 25:40 states outright: worship is received, not devised. The modern instinct in the opposite direction is not usually argued but assumed — that the shape of corporate worship is a matter of taste, effectiveness, or era, so long as the heart is right. The snuffdish answers it. God cared what the trimmings of the lamp were carried in, because the light was His and the house was His, and a heart right toward God is a heart content to be told how to come.
roots_summary: Hebrew machtah (H4289), a censer, firepan, snuffdish — the same word rendered three ways by function; melqachayim (H4457), the tongs or snuffers.
roots_lines: Hebrew machtah (H4289) — firepan, censer, snuffdish; Exodus 25:38, 37:23, Numbers 4:9, Leviticus 16:12.
Hebrew melqachayim (H4457) — tongs, snuffers; Exodus 25:38, Isaiah 6:6.
Hebrew menorah (H4501) — candlestick, lampstand; Exodus 25:31, Zechariah 4:2.
Hebrew tabniyth (H8403) — pattern, model, figure; Exodus 25:9, 25:40, 1 Chronicles 28:11.
Greek hupodeigma (G5262) — example, copy; Hebrews 8:5, 9:23.
usage: “The tongs thereof, and the snuffdishes thereof, shall be of pure gold” — gold for the least utensil of the light.
“His lamps, and his tongs, and his snuffdishes” — carried covered, on Levite shoulders.
“Look that thou make them after their pattern” — the reason every detail was given.

pos: n. (the scribe's writing case worn at the girdle; Hebrew qeseth)
etymology: English ink + horn, from the horn vessel in which ink was carried at the belt. The Hebrew names it simply the scribe's case, worn “by his side.”
biblical_def: Ezekiel saw six men come with slaughter weapons, “and one man among them was clothed with linen, with a writer's inkhorn by his side” (Eze 9:2). To that man the glory of God spoke: “And he called to the man clothed with linen, which had the writer's inkhorn by his side” (Eze 9:3). His commission was not to kill but to mark: “set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof” (Eze 9:4). And when the work was done he came back and said so: “I have done as thou hast commanded me” (Eze 9:11). Among six swords there was one pen, and the pen went first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an inkhorn as a small vessel used to hold ink, formerly of horn, and by extension a portable case for writing instruments.
webster_full: INKHORN, n. A small vessel used to hold ink on a writing table or desk, or for carrying it about; originally made of horn, whence the name.
INK, n. A black liquor or substance used for writing, generally made of an infusion of galls, copperas and gum arabic.
scriptures: Eze 9:2

And, behold, six men came from the way of the higher gate, which lieth toward the north, and every man a slaughter weapon in his hand; and one man among them was clothed with linen, with a writer's inkhorn by his side: and they went in, and stood beside the brasen altar.
Eze 9:3

And the glory of the God of Israel was gone up from the cherub, whereupon he was, to the threshold of the house. And he called to the man clothed with linen, which had the writer's inkhorn by his side;
Eze 9:4

And the LORD said unto him, Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and set a mark upon the foreheads of the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations that be done in the midst thereof.
Eze 9:11
And, behold, the man clothed with linen, which had the inkhorn by his side, reported the matter, saying, I have done as thou hast commanded me.
corruption_summary: The inkhorn marks a remnant before the sword falls, and the mark is set on men who grieve over sin the city has learned to enjoy.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 9 is the discriminating judgment of God set out in a single image. Six executioners, one scribe; and the scribe goes first, because God knows His own and will not slay the righteous with the wicked. The test is exact and it is inward: the mark falls on “the men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations.” Not the men who protest, organize, or separate — the men who grieve. Sighing over the sin of one's own city is presented here as the visible evidence of a heart still God's in a place that has abandoned Him, and Revelation 7:3 takes up the same sealing before the same kind of judgment.

The corruption to name is the loss of grief. A church can retain doctrine, ordinances, and vocabulary while losing entirely the capacity to mourn over what surrounds it, and a settled cheerfulness about a culture's abominations is not the fruit of the Spirit but the numbness Ezekiel is writing against. The opposite error is as real: grief that curdles into contempt, mourning that enjoys itself. The man with the inkhorn does not gloat and does not shrug. He weeps, he marks, and he reports that he has done as he was commanded.
roots_summary: Hebrew qeseth (H7083), a scribe's inkstand or writing case; tav (H8420), the mark set on the forehead; anach (H584), to sigh or groan.
roots_lines: Hebrew qeseth (H7083) — inkhorn, writer's case; Ezekiel 9:2, 9:3, 9:11 only.
Hebrew tav (H8420) — a mark, signature; Ezekiel 9:4, 9:6, Job 31:35.
Hebrew anach (H584) — to sigh, groan; Ezekiel 9:4, 21:6, Lamentations 1:4.
Hebrew badd (H906) — linen, the priestly cloth; Ezekiel 9:2, Leviticus 16:4, Daniel 10:5.
Greek sphragizo (G4972) — to seal, mark for ownership; Revelation 7:3, Ephesians 1:13.
usage: “A writer's inkhorn by his side” — one pen among six swords, and the pen goes first.
“The men that sigh and that cry for all the abominations” — the mark falls on grief.
“I have done as thou hast commanded me” — the scribe's whole report.

pos: n. (a costly timber shipped from Lebanon and Ophir for the temple; also spelled almug)
etymology: Hebrew algummim, of uncertain species — long identified with red sandalwood or a hard aromatic wood. Chronicles spells it algum, Kings almug; one timber, two transpositions.
biblical_def: Solomon wrote to Huram, “Send me also cedar trees, fir trees, and algum trees, out of Lebanon” (2Ch 2:8). The fleets brought more: “the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir, brought algum trees and precious stones” (2Ch 9:10). And the king spent it on the house of God first and his own house second: “the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers” (2Ch 9:11). Kings adds the verdict of scarcity: “there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day” (1Ki 10:12). The rarest wood in the world went into stairs men walked on and instruments men sang with.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) treats algum or almug as the name of a tree brought from Ophir and Lebanon for Solomon's work, generally supposed to be a species of sandalwood.
webster_full: ALMUG, ALGUM, n. In scripture, a tree or wood about which interpreters differ; generally supposed to be the red sandal wood, brought from Ophir and from Lebanon for the temple and the king's house.
TIMBER, n. That sort of wood which is proper for buildings or for tools, utensils, furniture and the like.
scriptures: Send me also cedar trees, fir trees, and algum trees, out of Lebanon: for I know that thy servants can skill to cut timber in Lebanon; and, behold, my servants shall be with thy servants,
And the servants also of Huram, and the servants of Solomon, which brought gold from Ophir, brought algum trees and precious stones.
And the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers: and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah.
And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD, and for the king's house, harps also and psalteries for singers: there came no such almug trees, nor were seen unto this day.
corruption_summary: The rarest timber on earth was spent on the house of God and on the instruments of praise, and Scripture records the order without apology.
corruption_paragraphs: Algum is a lesson in the direction of costliness. The wood came from Lebanon and from Ophir, at the end of a three-year voyage, and it was never seen again in that quantity. What was done with it? Terraces for the house of the LORD, then the palace, then harps and psalteries for the singers. Praise was worth the world's most expensive material. The same instinct puts alabaster on Christ's feet in John 12 and hears the objection that it might have been sold, and the same answer stands: what is spent on God is not wasted.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that costliness in worship is measured by what is given, not by what is displayed. Solomon's algum is not a warrant for opulence as such — the temple was a commanded and typological house, and the New Testament locates the glory in the assembled people rather than the building. But the reflex that treats every expense on the worship of God as money misdirected has no footing in either Testament, and Chronicles quietly records that the singers got the best wood in the world for their harps.
roots_summary: Hebrew algummim / almuggim (H418, H484), a precious timber; mesillah (H4546), a raised way or terrace; kinnowr (H3658), the harp.
roots_lines: Hebrew almuggim (H484) — almug trees; 1 Kings 10:11, 10:12.
Hebrew algummim (H418) — algum trees; 2 Chronicles 2:8, 9:10, 9:11.
Hebrew mesillah (H4546) — highway, terrace, raised way; 2 Chronicles 9:11, Isaiah 40:3.
Hebrew kinnowr (H3658) — harp; 2 Chronicles 9:11, Psalm 33:2, 1 Samuel 16:23.
Hebrew nebel (H5035) — psaltery, lute; 2 Chronicles 9:11, Psalm 144:9.
usage: “Send me also cedar trees, fir trees, and algum trees, out of Lebanon” — the temple order.
“Brought algum trees and precious stones” — the Ophir fleet's cargo.
“Harps and psalteries for singers” — the rarest wood spent on praise.

pos: n. (the glowing metallic colour at the centre of Ezekiel's visions of the glory; Hebrew chashmal)
etymology: Through French from Arabic anbar. The KJV uses it for Hebrew chashmal, a word found only in Ezekiel — a bright burnished alloy glowing like fire, rendered electrum in the Greek.
biblical_def: Amber in Scripture is never a stone and never an ornament; it is the colour of the glory. At the opening of the visions: “out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” (Eze 1:4). At the centre of the throne: “And I saw as the colour of amber, as the appearance of fire round about within it” (Eze 1:27). And again when the prophet is carried to Jerusalem: “as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber” (Eze 8:2). Ezekiel piles up as and appearance and likeness because he is describing what cannot be described, and he ends where the whole vision was going: “This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face” (Eze 1:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amber as a hard, semi-pellucid substance, tasteless and without smell except when heated, of a yellowish colour, susceptible of a fine polish.
webster_full: AMBER, n. A hard semi-pellucid substance, tasteless and without smell, except when pounded or heated, when it emits a fragrant odor. It is found in alluvial soils, or on the sea shore.
AMBER, a. Consisting of amber; resembling amber; as an amber-colored liquor.
scriptures: Eze 1:4

And I looked, and, behold, a whirlwind came out of the north, a great cloud, and a fire infolding itself, and a brightness was about it, and out of the midst thereof as the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire.
Eze 1:27

And I saw as the colour of amber, as the appearance of fire round about within it, from the appearance of his loins even upward, and from the appearance of his loins even downward, I saw as it were the appearance of fire, and it had brightness round about.
Eze 8:2

Then I beheld, and lo a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins even downward, fire; and from his loins even upward, as the appearance of brightness, as the colour of amber.
Eze 1:28

As the appearance of the bow that is in the cloud in the day of rain, so was the appearance of the brightness round about. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face, and I heard a voice of one that spake.
corruption_summary: Ezekiel's hedged language is reverence, not vagueness, and the right response to the glory is the one he gives: he fell on his face.
corruption_paragraphs: The chain of qualifiers in Ezekiel 1 — the appearance of the likeness of the glory — is often read as though the prophet were unsure of what he saw. He was not. He was certain of what he saw and certain that human speech could not carry it, and so he laid one comparison on another and refused to say that any of them was the thing itself. This is the creaturely reserve that the second commandment protects. God may show His glory; man may not fix it in an image. Ezekiel gives us colour and fire and a bow in the cloud, and then he gives us his face on the ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the vision ends in worship and not in curiosity. There is a long tradition of mining Ezekiel 1 for a diagram — the wheels, the faces, the amber all charted, dated, and assigned — and a shorter modern one of mining it for spectacle. Both stop where Ezekiel does not stop. The prophet who saw the throne fell on his face and then heard a voice, and the voice sent him to preach to a rebellious house. Glory seen and not obeyed has been misread.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashmal (H2830), a glowing brightness or burnished metal, only in Ezekiel; kabod (H3519), glory, weight; nogah (H5051), brightness.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashmal (H2830) — amber, glowing metal; Ezekiel 1:4, 1:27, 8:2 only.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; Ezekiel 1:28, Exodus 33:18, Isaiah 6:3.
Hebrew nogah (H5051) — brightness, shining; Ezekiel 1:4, 1:27, Habakkuk 3:4.
Hebrew demuth (H1823) — likeness, similitude; Ezekiel 1:5, 1:28, Genesis 1:26.
Hebrew mareh (H4758) — appearance, vision; Ezekiel 1:27, 1:28, Numbers 12:8.
usage: “As the colour of amber, out of the midst of the fire” — the glory at the storm's centre.
“The appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD” — reverence in the grammar.
“And when I saw it, I fell upon my face” — the only fit response.

pos: n. (the small chest the Philistines set beside the ark to carry their trespass offering; Hebrew argaz)
etymology: Old French cofre, a chest, from Latin cophinus. The Hebrew argaz occurs only in the ark narrative of 1 Samuel 6 — a box, a saddle-chest, set alongside and never upon the ark.
biblical_def: The Philistines, plagued for seven months, were told by their own priests how to send the ark home: “put the jewels of gold, which ye return him for a trespass offering, in a coffer by the side thereof” (1Sa 6:8). So it was done: “they laid the ark of the LORD upon the cart, and the coffer with the mice of gold and the images of their emerods” (1Sa 6:11). At Bethshemesh the Levites did the one thing the Philistines could not: “the Levites took down the ark of the LORD, and the coffer that was with it, wherein the jewels of gold were” (1Sa 6:15). And then the men of that town looked into the ark, and God smote them (1Sa 6:19). The coffer stood beside the ark; nothing was ever set upon it or looked into it and went unpunished.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a coffer as a chest or trunk, especially one for holding money or valuables, and by extension a treasury.
webster_full: COFFER, n. A chest or trunk; and as chests are used for keeping money, a coffer is used for a money chest, and coffers, in the plural, for treasure or funds.
COFFER, v.t. To put in a coffer; to hoard up.
scriptures: And take the ark of the LORD, and lay it upon the cart; and put the jewels of gold, which ye return him for a trespass offering, in a coffer by the side thereof; and send it away, that it may go.
And they laid the ark of the LORD upon the cart, and the coffer with the mice of gold and the images of their emerods.

And the Levites took down the ark of the LORD, and the coffer that was with it, wherein the jewels of gold were, and put them on the great stone: and the men of Bethshemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed sacrifices the same day unto the LORD.

And he smote the men of Bethshemesh, because they had looked into the ark of the LORD, even he smote of the people fifty thousand and threescore and ten men: and the people lamented, because the LORD had smitten many of the people with a great slaughter.
corruption_summary: The coffer beside the ark is the picture of an offering the heathen knew to send and a holiness they did not dare to touch.
corruption_paragraphs: Two things are remarkable about the Philistine coffer. The first is that pagans handled the ark more carefully than Israel did. They would not open it, they set their gold beside it and not in it, and their diviners told them plainly to give glory to the God of Israel. The second is what happened at Bethshemesh, where covenant people looked in and died. Privilege does not soften holiness; it sharpens accountability. Amos states the principle: you only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

The corruption to name is familiarity. The men of Bethshemesh had grown up with the ark as an idea and met it as a fact, and the fact killed them. A church can carry the vocabulary of the presence of God for generations while losing every trace of fear, and the surest sign of it is a settled confidence that God does not mind. Uzza reaches out his hand in 2 Samuel 6 with the best of intentions and dies for it. Holiness is not cruelty; it is the truth about God, and the gospel does not abolish it but satisfies it in the blood of Christ, through whom alone we come boldly.
roots_summary: Hebrew argaz (H712), a box or coffer, only in 1 Samuel 6; asham (H817), trespass offering; aron (H727), the ark or chest.
roots_lines: Hebrew argaz (H712) — coffer, box; 1 Samuel 6:8, 6:11, 6:15 only.
Hebrew asham (H817) — trespass offering, guilt; 1 Samuel 6:8, Leviticus 5:15.
Hebrew aron (H727) — ark, chest, coffin; 1 Samuel 6:8, Exodus 25:10, Genesis 50:26.
Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to smite, strike; 1 Samuel 6:19, Exodus 12:23.
Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory; 1 Samuel 6:5, 4:21.
usage: “In a coffer by the side thereof” — beside the ark, never upon it.
“The coffer with the mice of gold” — a heathen trespass offering.
“Because they had looked into the ark of the LORD” — the cost of familiarity.

pos: n. (the wedding hall; “children of the bridechamber” = the bridegroom's wedding party; Greek numphon)
etymology: English bride + chamber, rendering Greek numphon, the room where the marriage was kept. The “children of the bridechamber” are the groom's companions, whose one duty for the seven days was gladness.
biblical_def: Asked why His disciples did not fast, Christ answered with a wedding: “Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast” (Mat 9:15). Mark and Luke record the same defence (Mar 2:19; Luk 5:34). The Baptist had already conceded the title: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice” (Joh 3:29). Christ is not merely at the feast. He is the Bridegroom, and the presence of the Bridegroom is itself the reason His people may not mourn.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bridechamber as the nuptial apartment, and notes the scriptural sense in which the children of the bridechamber are the friends attending the bridegroom.
webster_full: BRIDECHAMBER, n. The nuptial apartment. Matt. ix.
BRIDEGROOM, n. A man newly married; or a man about to be married.
BRIDE, n. A woman newly married, or about to be married.
scriptures: Mat 9:15

And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? but the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then shall they fast.
Mar 2:19
And Jesus said unto them, Can the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them? as long as they have the bridegroom with them, they cannot fast.
Luk 5:34
And he said unto them, Can ye make the children of the bridechamber fast, while the bridegroom is with them?
Joh 3:29
He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom's voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled.
corruption_summary: Christ claims the Bridegroom's title, and with it a claim to deity, since in the prophets the husband of Israel is the LORD Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The bridechamber saying is one of the quietest and largest claims Christ makes. Throughout the prophets the Bridegroom of Israel is God — thy Maker is thine husband, in Isaiah 54; the betrothal of Hosea 2; the marriage covenant broken in Jeremiah 3. When Jesus explains His disciples' joy by saying that the Bridegroom is with them, He is not borrowing a pleasant figure. He is taking the place the LORD occupies in the prophets, and John the Baptist confirms the arrangement by naming himself only the friend. This is why fasting was suspended: not because fasting is obsolete, but because the Husband of the church was standing in the room.

The correction to make is against sentimental use of the bride imagery. Ephesians 5 grounds it in Christ's self-giving and the church's subjection, and Revelation 19 in the Lamb's marriage after judgment falls — the figure is covenantal, not romantic, and it carries authority and cost along with love. It also carries a calendar. Christ Himself said the days would come when the Bridegroom is taken away and His people would fast; the church between the ascension and the marriage supper lives in those days, glad in a present Lord by faith and hungry for a Lord present in sight.
roots_summary: Greek numphon (G3567), the bridal chamber; numphios (G3566), bridegroom; numphe (G3565), bride.
roots_lines: Greek numphon (G3567) — bridechamber; Matthew 9:15, Mark 2:19, Luke 5:34.
Greek numphios (G3566) — bridegroom; Matthew 9:15, John 3:29, Matthew 25:1.
Greek numphe (G3565) — bride, daughter in law; John 3:29, Revelation 19:7, 21:9.
Greek nesteuo (G3522) — to fast; Matthew 9:15, Mark 2:19, Acts 13:2.
Hebrew baal (H1166) — to marry, be master of; Isaiah 54:5, Jeremiah 3:14.
usage: “Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?”
“The days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken from them” — fasting has a season.
“The friend of the bridegroom” — the Baptist's whole estimate of himself.

pos: n. (the furnace in which bricks were burnt; a place of forced labour and of judgment; Hebrew malben)
etymology: English brick + kiln, from Latin culina, a stove. The Hebrew malben is the brick-mould or the place of brick-making — the tool and the yard together.
biblical_def: The brickkiln in Scripture is always bound up with bondage or judgment. David dealt so with the Ammonites: he “made them pass through the brickkiln” (2Sa 12:31). Jeremiah was told to bury stones “in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes” (Jer 43:9), so that Nebuchadnezzar's throne might one day stand on the very pavement where Judah's refugees had trusted Egypt. Nahum mocks Nineveh with it: “go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln” (Nah 3:14). Behind all of it stands Egypt, where they “made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick” (Exo 1:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brickkiln as a kiln or furnace in which bricks are baked or burnt, and a kiln as a fabric of brick or stone for the purpose of burning or drying.
webster_full: BRICKKILN, n. A kiln or furnace in which bricks are baked or burnt; or a pile of bricks laid loose, with arches underneath to receive the wood or fuel.
BRICK, n. A mass of earth, chiefly clay, first moistened and made fine by kneading, then formed into a long square in a mould, dried and baked.
KILN, n. A fabric of brick or stone, which may be heated for the purpose of hardening, burning or drying any thing.
scriptures: And he brought forth the people that were therein, and put them under saws, and under harrows of iron, and under axes of iron, and made them pass through the brickkiln: and thus did he unto all the cities of the children of Ammon. So David and all the people returned unto Jerusalem.
Jer 43:9
Take great stones in thine hand, and hide them in the clay in the brickkiln, which is at the entry of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah;
Nah 3:14
Draw thee waters for the siege, fortify thy strong holds: go into clay, and tread the morter, make strong the brickkiln.
Exo 1:14
And they made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in morter, and in brick, and in all manner of service in the field: all their service, wherein they made them serve, was with rigour.
corruption_summary: Judah fled to Egypt for safety and Jeremiah buried stones in Pharaoh's brickyard to mark the spot where the conqueror would set his throne.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 43 is one of the bitterest ironies in the prophets. The remnant had been told plainly to stay in the land; they went down to Egypt instead, dragging Jeremiah with them, and the first thing God had him do on arrival was hide stones in the brick pavement at Tahpanhes and announce that Nebuchadnezzar would spread his royal pavilion over them. The refuge chosen against the word of God became the platform of the judgment they fled. Egypt is Scripture's standing name for that transaction — a house of bondage that always looks like shelter from a distance.

The corruption to name is the search for a political refuge from a spiritual verdict. Isaiah spent chapters on it: woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and look not unto the Holy One of Israel. The modern form is not usually a treaty but a strategy — the conviction that the church's safety lies in an alliance, a majority, or a technique, and that the word which called for repentance can be answered with a plan. Jeremiah's stones are still under the pavement of every such arrangement.
roots_summary: Hebrew malben (H4404), brickkiln, brick-mould; lebenah (H3843), a brick; chomer (H2563), clay or morter.

Hebrew lebenah (H3843) — brick; Exodus 1:14, 5:7, Genesis 11:3.
Hebrew chomer (H2563) — clay, morter, heap; Exodus 1:14, Nahum 3:14, Isaiah 64:8.
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, bondage, labour; Exodus 1:14, 2:23.
Hebrew perek (H6531) — rigour, harshness; Exodus 1:14, Leviticus 25:43.
usage: “Hide them in the clay in the brickkiln” — a throne foretold in a brickyard.
“Go into clay, and tread the morter” — Nahum's mockery of Nineveh's defences.
“In morter, and in brick” — the bitterness of Egypt.

pos: n. pl. (the twisted chain work covering the capitals of the temple pillars; Hebrew sarsar, gedilah)
etymology: Old English writha, a twisted band, from writhan, to twist. In the temple account the wreaths are chain work — interlaced metal cordage — not garlands of leaves.
biblical_def: Hiram's work on the two pillars is described in detail: “nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter” (1Ki 7:17). Chronicles counts them again with the pommels: “the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars” (2Ch 4:12), and adds the fruit: “four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath” (2Ch 4:13). Kings gives the same care to the network and its rows (1Ki 7:18). Two free-standing pillars, holding up nothing, crowned with chains and fruit at the door of the house of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a wreath as something twisted or curled; a garland or chaplet; and in architecture, ornamental work twisted or interlaced.
webster_full: WREATH, n. Something twisted; a garland; a chaplet; as a wreath of flowers.
WREATH, n. In architecture, an ornament of twisted or interlaced work, as of chains or cords.
CHAPITER, n. The upper part or capital of a column or pillar.
scriptures: And nets of checker work, and wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters which were upon the top of the pillars; seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other chapiter.
And he made the pillars, and two rows round about upon the one network, to cover the chapiters that were upon the top, with pomegranates: and so did he for the other chapiter.

To wit, the two pillars, and the pommels, and the chapiters which were on the top of the two pillars, and the two wreaths to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were on the top of the pillars;
And four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths; two rows of pomegranates on each wreath, to cover the two pommels of the chapiters which were upon the pillars.
corruption_summary: Scripture spends four passages on ornament that bore no weight, because beauty in the house of God is not waste.
corruption_paragraphs: Jachin and Boaz upheld no roof. They stood before the porch as signs — He shall establish, in Him is strength — and their capitals were dressed with chain work and four hundred pomegranates. The Holy Spirit thought this worth recording twice, in Kings and again in Chronicles, with the counts. That is a rebuke to the utilitarian instinct in worship, which asks of every element what it accomplishes. Some things in the house of God are there to say something true about God, and saying it is the whole of their function.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the regulative principle governs the elements of worship, not the beauty of them. What God has commanded is required and what He has not commanded is not permitted — but within what He commands, Scripture never treats care, skill, and loveliness as suspect. Bezaleel was filled with the Spirit of God to cut stones and carve timber. A bare aesthetic is not a purer one, and the pomegranates on the wreaths are in the text on purpose.
roots_summary: Hebrew sarsar (H8331), chain work, wreathed work; gedilah (H1434), twisted threads, wreaths; kothereth (H3805), the chapiter or crown of a pillar.
roots_lines: Hebrew sarsar (H8331) — chain work, wreath; 1 Kings 7:17, 2 Chronicles 4:12.
Hebrew gedilah (H1434) — twisted threads, fringes, wreaths; Deuteronomy 22:12, 1 Kings 7:17.
Hebrew kothereth (H3805) — chapiter, capital of a pillar; 1 Kings 7:16, 2 Chronicles 4:12.
Hebrew rimmon (H7416) — pomegranate; 2 Chronicles 4:13, Exodus 28:33.
Hebrew sebakah (H7639) — network, lattice; 1 Kings 7:17, 2 Kings 25:17.
usage: “Wreaths of chain work, for the chapiters” — metal cordage, not garlands.
“Four hundred pomegranates on the two wreaths” — counted, and recorded twice.
“Seven for the one chapiter, and seven for the other” — the number of completeness.

pos: n. pl. (the large body-shields of Solomon's guard and Asa's army; Hebrew tsinnah)
etymology: Old French targette, diminutive of targe, a shield. In the KJV target renders the great shield that covered the whole man, distinguished from the smaller buckler.
biblical_def: “And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target” (1Ki 10:16), and Chronicles repeats the record (2Ch 9:15). Asa's army carried them into battle: “Asa had an army of men that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand” (2Ch 14:8). But gold shields are only as safe as the kingdom that holds them, and within five years of Solomon's death Shishak came: “he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made” (1Ki 14:26). Rehoboam replaced them with brass, and the guard went on carrying them as though nothing had changed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a target as a shield or buckler of a small size, or a species of shield used in war, borne on the arm to protect the body.
webster_full: TARGET, n. A shield or buckler of a small size, or a sort of shield used as a defense against arrows and other weapons.
SHIELD, n. A broad piece of defensive armor; a buckler; used in war for the protection of the body.
scriptures: And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of gold went to one target.
And king Solomon made two hundred targets of beaten gold: six hundred shekels of beaten gold went to one target.

And Asa had an army of men that bare targets and spears, out of Judah three hundred thousand; and out of Benjamin, that bare shields and drew bows, two hundred and fourscore thousand: all these were mighty men of valour.
And he took away the treasures of the house of the LORD, and the treasures of the king's house; he even took away all: and he took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made.
corruption_summary: Gold shields taken and brass shields hung in their place, carried with the same ceremony — the exact picture of a religion that keeps the forms after the substance is gone.
corruption_paragraphs: The story of Solomon's targets does not end in 1 Kings 10; it ends in 1 Kings 14. Shishak carried the gold away, Rehoboam made brass ones to replace them, and the guard bore them before the king exactly as before. The procession looked identical. That is the sharpest picture in the historical books of a house that has lost its treasure and kept its liturgy, and it took only five years. Glory departs quietly, and the men carrying the shields are usually the last to know.

The corruption to name is substitution without confession. Nobody in Jerusalem announced that the shields were now brass; the ceremony simply continued. Churches and denominations have done the same with the doctrines they were built on — the language of substitutionary atonement retained over a moral-example theory, the language of inspiration retained over a text now handled as a human artifact, the language of holiness retained over a therapeutic ethic. Rehoboam's brass is what orthodoxy becomes when it is kept as vocabulary. The remedy is not a better ceremony but repentance and the recovery of the gold.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsinnah (H6793), the great shield covering the body; magen (H4043), the smaller buckler; shalat (H7982), shields of gold.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsinnah (H6793) — large shield, target; 1 Kings 10:16, 2 Chronicles 14:8, Psalm 35:2.
Hebrew magen (H4043) — buckler, small shield; 2 Chronicles 14:8, Genesis 15:1, Psalm 3:3.
Hebrew shalat (H7982) — shield, quiver; 2 Samuel 8:7, 2 Kings 11:10.
Hebrew zahab shachut — beaten gold; 1 Kings 10:16, 10:17.
Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — brass, copper; 1 Kings 14:27, Exodus 27:2.
usage: “Two hundred targets of beaten gold” — Solomon's guard at its height.
“Men that bare targets and spears” — Asa's three hundred thousand.
“He took away all the shields of gold which Solomon had made” — five years later.

pos: v. (bound about with silver bands; of the pillars of the tabernacle court; Hebrew chashaq)
etymology: From fillet, Old French filet, a little thread or band, from Latin filum, a thread. The Hebrew chashaq means to bind, join, or fasten — and elsewhere, to cleave to in love.
biblical_def: Of the sixty pillars round the court the command was: “All the pillars round about the court shall be filleted with silver; their hooks shall be of silver, and their sockets of brass” (Exo 27:17). The work was done as commanded: “the hooks of the pillars and their fillets of silver” and “all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver” (Exo 38:17). The silver came from the redemption money of the numbered men, and what was left over “he made hooks for the pillars, and overlaid their chapiters, and filleted them” (Exo 38:28). Those pillars carried the hangings that walled the court: “there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side” (Exo 27:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fillet as a little band to tie about the hair, and in architecture a little square member or ornament used in divers places, and to fillet as to bind with a fillet.
webster_full: FILLET, n. A little band to tie about the hair of the head. In architecture, a little square member or ornament used in divers places, but generally as a corona over a greater molding.
FILLET, v.t. To bind with a fillet or little band.
SOCKET, n. Any hollow thing or place which receives and holds something else.
scriptures: All the pillars round about the court shall be filleted with silver; their hooks shall be of silver, and their sockets of brass.

And the sockets for the pillars were of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets of silver; and the overlaying of their chapiters of silver; and all the pillars of the court were filleted with silver.
And of the thousand seven hundred seventy and five shekels he made hooks for the pillars, and overlaid their chapiters, and filleted them.
Exo 27:9
And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:
corruption_summary: The bands that held the court together were made of the redemption money, so that the enclosure of the sanctuary was literally bound with the price of ransomed men.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 38 gives the accounting. The silver of the tabernacle came from the half shekel paid by every man numbered in the census — the atonement money of Exodus 30, a ransom for his soul. That silver became the sockets the boards stood in and the fillets that bound the pillars of the court. The house of God rested on redemption money and was bound about with redemption money, and the typology is not subtle: the church is founded and held together by a price paid for souls. Peter draws the line himself — not with silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the unity of God's people is a purchased unity, not a negotiated one. The fillets did not create the court; they bound pillars that were already set in their sockets, in the place and order commanded. Modern instincts run the other way, treating unity as something the church manufactures by minimizing what divides. Exodus 27 will not have it. The pillars stand where they were put, on the sockets they were given, and the silver that binds them was paid for men.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashaq (H2836), to bind, fillet, and also to cleave to in love; chashuq (H2838), fillets, bands; kopher (H3724), ransom, atonement money.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashaq (H2836) — to bind, fillet, to long for; Exodus 27:17, 38:28, Deuteronomy 7:7.
Hebrew chashuq (H2838) — fillets, bands of the pillars; Exodus 27:10, 38:17.
Hebrew kopher (H3724) — ransom, atonement price; Exodus 30:12, Numbers 35:31.
Hebrew eden (H134) — socket, base; Exodus 38:27, 26:19.
Hebrew ammud (H5982) — pillar, column; Exodus 27:17, 1 Kings 7:15.
usage: “All the pillars round about the court shall be filleted with silver” — the command.
“All the pillars of the court were filleted with silver” — the obedience.
“He made hooks for the pillars… and filleted them” — the redemption money spent.
